Catastrophe data aggregator PERILS AG has updated its estimate of insurance industry losses for the severe convective storms (SCS) that swept across Germany, France, Switzerland, and Italy in Europe between July 13th and 19th, 2026, lifting the total to EUR 2.806 billion.

The storms are also known as “SCS Cerry”, following the naming of an associated low-pressure system by the Free University of Berlin.

PERILS published its initial industry loss estimate for the severe convective storms in late August, putting the total at EUR 2.186 billion.

As we said at the time, this outbreak of severe convective storms (SCS) across Europe became the largest loss from that peril in Europe in the PERILS AG list of loss events.

It also marked the largest insurance industry loss estimate for any European catastrophe event that PERILS has issued since the series of European windstorms in February 2022.

Now in its second industry loss estimate from the event, PERILS has lifted the total by roughly 28% to EUR 2.806 billion.

PERILS explained that its loss estimate is based on data gathered from impacted insurers, including losses from property and motor lines of business.

PERILS will also publish a third estimate of the market loss from the mid-July severe convective storms on January 19th, 2027, six months after the event end date.

Earlier this week, PERILS also published its initial loss estimate for the severe convective storm and hail outbreak that struck parts of western Europe between August 26th and 28th 2026, placing the total at EUR 3,296 million.

This event, combined with the July outbreak, showcases how costly European SCS activity has been in recent months.

At the same time, CatIQ, Canada’s insured loss and exposure indices provider and subsidiary of PERILS, has published its second industry loss estimate for the severe convective storms that struck southern Ontario, including Toronto, on September 2nd and 3rd, 2026, lifting the total to CAD $671 million.

CatIQ published its initial loss estimate from the event earlier this month, putting the total at $563 million.

With claims having continued to be filed, the total has risen steadily now, increasing by roughly 19% to $671 million for the second industry loss estimate. CatIQ’s loss number covers both property and motor lines of business.

The company also confirmed that it will publish its third loss estimate of the market loss from the southern Ontario SCS on December 3rd, 2026, three months after the event end date.

Luzi Hitz, Product Manager at PERILS, commented: “These two loss updates show clearly that severe convective storms are a major risk for the insurance markets in Europe and Canada. In fact, in recent years most mid-latitude countries globally have experienced more severe losses from convective storms than previously.

“There are multiple factors driving this. Firstly, this reflects the increase in vulnerable assets such as solar panels, roof windows, light-weight blinds and soft external wall insulation. Also, as economies grow there are simply more assets at risk of damage. Finally, the warming climate is driving an increase in the formation of more violent and damaging SCS events.”

Caroline Floyd, Director of CatIQ, said: “Severe convective storms have again been at the forefront of what has been a very active year for Canadian catastrophes. More than half of the year’s events involved SCS, including multiple major catastrophes affecting large population centres. The growing global impacts of this peril reaffirm the importance of having accurate data detailing the effects of these kinds of events.”

Arbol, the technology-led underwriter of parametric risk transfer, climate, and weather re/insurance business, has designed a parametric product that aims to transfer the risk of government-imposed moratoriums on data center construction projects.

The parametric insurance is designed to protect against the regulatory risk of government halting or suspending data center construction as a class, rather than site-specific permit denials.

Arbol believes it to be the first insurance product designed to cover the regulatory risk that traditional insurance products typically miss and it will payout a predetermined amount if a covered action stays in effect past an agreed waiting period, with parametric trigger and settlement based on information from the public record.

Arbol’s new product is named Data Center Regulatory Moratorium Cover and it is seen as a beneficial addition to the data center insurance product complex, in being able to protect the capital already committed to a project and the carrying costs that can accumulate while construction efforts sit idle.

“Data center development has a new and fast-growing risk, and until now there was no way to transfer it,” explained Sid Jha, founder and CEO of Arbol. “A moratorium or construction hold can strand hundreds of millions in committed capital, and standard policies do not respond. We pay objectively when a government action halts a project, which turns an unpredictable regulatory exposure into one developers and their lenders can plan around.”

It’s a novel parametric risk transfer product, being focused on insuring a source of regulatory risk that traditional covers typically seek to avoid.

The company explained, “Regulatory risk of this kind has long been considered uninsurable. A government action produces no physical loss and has sat outside the reach of standard insurance, which has left developers to lobby it, litigate it or absorb it. Arbol brought the exposure into a transferable form by applying the specialty underwriting and alternative-capital capabilities it uses across other classes the market finds difficult to write.”

Arbol’s new parametric Data Center Regulatory Moratorium Cover is now available to data center developers through brokers, it may also be relevant to the investors or capital providers backing the artificial intelligence (AI) data center build-out.

Arbol noted, “The exposure is growing and has moved from state houses to county boards. State moratorium bills have drawn most of the attention and many have failed, while the binding constraints are local. As of August 2026 there were 45 state-level measures across 36 states and restrictions in 194 local jurisdictions. In a Gallup survey conducted in March 2026, 71% of Americans said they oppose construction of an AI data center in their own area, with 48% strongly opposed.”

Over the years we’ve seen a number of parametric risk transfer products that utilise trigger and settlement data from public record and government pronouncement. But this is the first time we’ve seen one focused on large-scale construction projects, which just serves to demonstrate how high-profile and in some cases contentious the AI data center build-out has become.

After the devastating impacts of hurricane Melissa triggered a full $150 million payout of its IBRD CAR Jamaica 2024 parametric catastrophe bond, the rapid funding from this insurance product helped the country recover its electricity network faster than would have otherwise been possible, the government’s Chief Fiscal Economist explained last week.

Speaking at the ILS Bermuda Convergence 2026 conference on the island last week, Terron Francis, Chief Fiscal Economist in the Ministry of Finance & the Public Service, Government of Jamaica highlighted the critical role of risk transfer and insurance risk capital in helping the Caribbean island nation to recover after the impactful storm.

It was enlightening to hear how the proceeds of the catastrophe bond payout were put to immediate use, in helping to restore power to the affected western regions of Jamaica.

This is a story seldom told in reinsurance and insurance-linked securities markets, that the vital capital sources are both critical for recovery and also help to buffer government budgets from much worse financial effects, when natural catastrophes strike.

Francis explained that Jamaica’s forward-thinking use of risk transfer and insurance to create a multi-layered disaster risk financing structure had helped to prevent the negative economic effects of the major hurricane landfall being much worse than they could have been without the protection.

Jamaica’s multi-layered risk-transfer arrangements included parametric insurance cover from the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF SPC) and the government’s second sponsorship of a catastrophe bond, facilitated by the World Bank.

These instruments worked as designed, responding to the impact of a high-severity, low-frequency return period catastrophe event.

Francis said that the parametric catastrophe bond payout arrived within 30 days, supporting response and recovery for Jamaica, without forcing the government into emergency borrowing or substantial programme-budget reallocations.

He presented Jamaica’s experience as evidence that well-structured and designed planned disaster risk financing can improve fiscal resilience and deliver social benefits, while reducing the fiscal economic burden that would have materialised without such risk transfer instruments being in place.

Francis explained, “The catastrophe bond paid out following Hurricane Melissa in 2025, yielding to the country $150 million US dollars.

“Now that is significant. It doesn’t close the gap, as it relates to the funding required for the response and recovery effort, but certainly it would have given the Jamaica government a significant boost in terms of its immediate response.

“In fact, the resources that we would have obtained from the triggering of these policies, the catastrophe bond, and those policies which we hold with the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility, those would have enabled Jamaica to provide assistance to the single electricity electricity supplier in Jamaica, the Jamaica Public Service Company (JPS), to enable them to accelerate the repairs to the network, which was significantly damaged, enabling them to restore electricity to businesses as well as to households much earlier than they would have anticipated.

“So when the hurricane hit in October of 2025, the power right across the western side of the of the island went at the time. JPS assessed that it would take, because of the significance of the damage to the power network, it would not be before July of 2026 that power would have been restored.

“However, with the assistance provided by the government, we had 98% of the western side of the island actually receiving power back by February, March of 2026. So we see how the investment in the catastrophe bond assisted Jamaica in restoring some economic activity to the west, particularly the western part of Jamaica, because for the eastern and central parts of Jamaica, those were not significantly damaged, and so there was continuous electricity being provided to that section.”

He went on to highlight how this protects government budgets and reduced the need for immediate borrowing, which is the more typical route for disaster recovery financing when high-severity events occur.

“With the payment of the triggered amounts from the catastrophe bond, the government of Jamaica was able to undertake its response, undertake some amount of recovery, without having to undertake much reallocation of its programme budget.

“Not only that, we did not have to engage in emergency borrowing, which normally is what happens following the aftermath of a hurricane, we would have had to resort to significant adjustments in the budget. We would have had to run to find creditors to provide us loans. But in this instance, we didn’t need to do that. So there was fiscal stability that was ensured, but also there was debt stability,” Francis said.

He further noted that Jamaica’s debt to GDP ratio only increased by a few percentage points, from around 62.4% to 65.5% after the event, where as more typically this could have soared if immediate borrowing was required to fund the necessary recovery.

Francis stated, “Now that is unprecedented. Usually there is a big jump in the public debt to GDP ratio following a natural disaster. So these are some of the benefits that Jamaica experienced from having invested primarily in the catastrophe bond, which triggered a full payout following the passage of Hurricane Melissa.”

He added, “We know that parametric insurance provides you fast, reliable disbursements, and so our investment in the catastrophe bond cemented that for us. That this is the way to go, rather than doing indemnity where persons have to come and do an assessment to see what the losses are. We were able to benefit from the payouts within under 30 days of the event actually impacting Jamaica.

“I believe that Jamaica, having demonstrated the effectiveness of a strategic disaster risk financing plan, that other disaster-prone territories, small island developing states in particular, that we would have provided evidence that it pays to have such a disaster risk financing plan and strategy in place. And I believe that, from a regional perspective, that scaling this ILS framework will be vital to securing resilience, particularly for the Caribbean area.”

It is good for the industry and its investors to hear how its risk capital is put to use by users of insurance-linked securities technology. As we said, it’s a story that is seldom told. It’s also positive for other potential sovereign sponsors of cat bonds to hear from this experience and how the funding was utilised.

More typically, we think of or hear about an insurer or reinsurer funding its claims payout to policyholders when a catastrophe bond is triggered, given the reinsurance protection they often are providing.

But Jamaica’s experience shows how cat bonds and ILS can be a critical component of sovereign disaster risk financing, providing vital funding to aid the immediate response to a disaster while protecting the economic and fiscal situation to reduce pressure as the recovery continues.

The catastrophe bond market has reached a scale where its continued growth actively reinforces the investment case, offering greater scalability, improved liquidity and broader scope to diversify within natural catastrophe risk, according to Dr. Rom Aviv of GAM Investments.

Aviv, who is well-known across the insurance-linked securities (ILS) industry, joined GAM Investments as Head of ILS in April 2025. 

In a recent article authored by Aviv, the executive states that while natural catastrophe events are unpredictable, the behaviour of the cat bond market has historically exhibited a consistent pattern, one that underpins the asset class’s investment case.

“From February 2002 to March 2026, the Swiss Re Cat Bond Total Return Index generated an annualised return of 7.7% with annualised volatility of 3.7%. Over the same period, US high yield returned 7.1% with 8.8% volatility, while the S&P 500 returned 9.6% with 14.8% volatility. Correlations between cat bonds and major traditional asset-class indices remained at or below 0.26. The index has recorded only one negative calendar year since inception: 2022,” Aviv said.

“Cat bonds may resemble fixed income operationally, but not economically. Their principal source of risk is not the solvency of a corporate borrower, the path of policy rates or economic growth. Instead, investors are paid to absorb defined insurance losses arising from natural catastrophes. The result is a return engine that has historically exhibited relatively low sensitivity to many of the common risk factors embedded in traditional portfolios.”

Aviv continued: “That distinction matters because the stock-bond hedge depends on the source of the shock. In March 2020, equities and corporate credit sold off together as liquidity disappeared. In 2022, inflation and aggressive monetary tightening produced simultaneous calendar-year losses for both US equities and the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. IMF research published in February 2026 noted that stocks and bonds have increasingly tended to sell off together during market stress since 2020.”

Importantly, while cat bonds can also experience drawdowns too, the key difference is what drives the losses: insured catastrophic events, as opposed to factors such as profitability fluctuations, financial leverage, interest rate sensitivity, or macroeconomic cycles.

Moreover, as the cat bond market continues to further expand, a key trend that has helped drive this momentum is how comfortable sponsors have become with the mechanics of the overall cat bond space, and it’s this familiarity that has ultimately encouraged a wave of new sponsors to venture into the space.

Cat bond issuance in H1 2026 hit a new high of almost $18 billion, up on last year’s previous record of $17.6 billion. The period also set issuance records for 144A property cat and total 144A issuance at $17.3 billion and $17.7 billion, respectively.

With the outstanding catastrophe bond market reaching $65.6 billion in H1 2026, it’s increasing depth is delivering benefits to investors.

“Repeat sponsors remain the backbone of issuance, but the universe continues to broaden across primary insurers, reinsurers, public-sector entities, geographies and perils. What began as a tactical solution has evolved into an established component of the global catastrophe risk-transfer market,” Aviv added.

Interestingly, Aviv further points out that some of the most compelling features of catastrophe bonds were not particularly designed for investors, and that they emerged solely because sponsors needed efficient, secure and capital-effective reinsurance protection.

Key amongst these is that cat bonds provide floating income with limited duration.

“The coupon generally has two components: a return on collateral and an insurance risk spread paid by the sponsor. Because the collateral is short-dated and resets with money-market rates, cat bonds behave economically more like floating-rate instruments than conventional fixed-rate bonds,” Aviv explained.

The executive noted that this feature was particularly valuable in 2022, where traditional bond portfolios suffered as yields rose and duration repriced. However, whilst this happened, cat bond investors managed to benefit from higher collateral income.

Aviv also acknowledges that most catastrophe bonds tend to mature around three years, commonly within a three-to-five-year range.

“Underlying insurance-policy risk periods are typically annual. That matters because catastrophe risk is not static: insured values change, models are recalibrated and the hazard itself evolves,” the executive said.

“Short maturities force the market to re-underwrite and reprice risk continuously. Investors are not locked for a decade into assumptions made at issuance. Major events have historically been followed by higher risk spreads and tighter available reinsurance capacity; a short-dated market allows investors to access that repricing quickly.”

Aviv added: “The market has reached a scale where its continued growth is supporting the investment case. The outstanding market reached roughly USD 65.6 billion in June 2026 after another record first half of issuance. As the market deepens, three benefits follow for investors: greater scalability, better liquidity and more scope to diversify catastrophe risk itself.”

Regarding scalability, Aviv notes that cat bond allocations that were difficult to implement a decade ago are increasingly practical today. This is demonstrated by UCITS cat bond funds managing to surpass $21 billion in assets in July 2026, while sponsor adoption continues to broaden.

The executive also added that regular primary issuance and a broader manager and investor base helps create more two-way flow, more observable pricing and stronger valuation discipline across the asset class.

The cat bond market also continues to broaden and expand from its main source of risk, that being US hurricane risk, with issuance broadening across earthquake, wildfire, severe convective storm, flood, European and Asian perils, as well as non-natural risks such as cyber.

“A Florida hurricane, a Japanese earthquake and a European windstorm have different physical drivers. A broader universe therefore allows managers to diversify catastrophe risk itself, not merely diversify away from financial-market risk,” Aviv said.

Concluding: “Cat bonds remain a specialist asset class. They carry real tail risk, model risk and event-driven liquidity risk. But after almost 25 years of observable performance, the central thesis has remained broadly intact: investors have historically been compensated for bearing a risk whose fundamental driver is largely independent of the macroeconomic risks embedded in most traditional portfolios. That has become increasingly difficult to replicate with traditional fixed income alone

“While natural catastrophes will remain unpredictable, the behaviour of a well-diversified portfolio of cat bonds may be considerably less so.”

The full report is now available to download from Artemis’ 2026 Monte Carlo Rendezvous Executive Roundtable. The event featured leading insurance-linked securities and reinsurance market experts discussing investor sentiment, market conditions, pricing discipline and emerging opportunities across the catastrophe bond and ILS landscape.

Held in September 2026, in partnership with SCOR Investment Partners and Vantage Risk, our sixth ILS-focused roundtable at the annual Monte Carlo reinsurance industry meeting brought together nine market leaders to share their insights and debate the issues shaping the asset class.

A full report of the 2026 Artemis Monte Carlo Executive Roundtable event is now available to download for free.

Discussions explored evolving investor appetite and sophistication, alongside the importance of continued education and stable pricing as ILS attracts growing interest and continues to mature.

The outlook for catastrophe bonds remained positive, with participants highlighting a healthy pipeline for the remainder of 2026 and into early 2027. Momentum was also viewed as strong across private ILS and blended strategies, underpinned by attractive risk-adjusted returns, diversification, and several years of strong performance.

However, as the reinsurance market continues to soften, maintaining underwriting and structural discipline is becoming increasingly important. Participants emphasised the need to remain focused on terms, attachment points and rate adequacy, while questioning whether spreads will stabilise before falling to levels that no longer adequately compensate investors.

The discussion also considered opportunities to expand ILS into other areas, including casualty, as well as the potential presented by data centre-related risks. Alongside these opportunities, participants examined what could disrupt the market’s positive trajectory or undermine investor confidence in catastrophe bonds and other ILS structures, even as investor familiarity with and understanding of the asset class continue to deepen.

While acknowledging the inherent challenges of predicting market direction, participants anticipated a constructive environment for ILS investors in 2027.

For this year’s Monte Carlo Rendez-Vous Executive Roundtable we were joined by the following participants:

  • Sidney Rostan, Head of Insurance-Linked Securities, SCOR Investment Partners.
  • Chris McKeown, Chief Executive, Reinsurance, ILS, and Innovation, Vantage Risk.
  • Kathleen Faries, CEO, Artex Capital Solutions.
  • Stephen A. Velotti, CEO, Pillar Capital Management.
  • Kate Tongue, Executive Director, Argenta Group.
  • Fergus Reynolds, Head of ILS, Cedar Trace.
  • John Modin, CEO, Mt. Logan Capital Management.
  • Andre Perez, Founder & CEO – Bermuda, Nascent Group.
  • Guillaume Courtet, Head of Portfolio Management ILS, Schroders Capital.

item.content:encoded:

As casualty sidecars continue to gain traction, rating agency AM Best has highlighted that clear exit mechanics, high-quality collateral, and transparent risk transfer are critical to lowering tail risk capital charges for sponsors, warning that uncertain exit terms or weak collateral can leave cedents holding unexpected residual risk.

In the report, AM Best notes that when a sponsor cedes business to a casualty sidecar, the protection provided by the transaction is limited by the sidecar’s capitalisation, and contractual features such as loss ratio caps.

The agency explained that it defines tail risk as the residual exposure borne by the sponsor when sidecar capital is insufficient to absorb losses exceeding expectations, directly influencing how much contingent exposure should reduce the sponsor’s available capital.

“Institutional investors, including the private capital involved in establishing these vehicles, generally require a defined path to liquidity. Transactions have started to converge on an exit term of about seven years. Culpeper Capital (one of the lead investors in George Street Re) has pointed to a degree of standardization around that time horizon, since reserves need to be reasonably seasoned before an exit valuation is credible,” said AM Best.

The agency importantly states that tail risk matters on both sides of casualty sidecar transactions, given that investors want finality, and cedents want to know what risks (if any), are commuted back to them when an exit is exercised.

“The market has now developed a set of exit mechanisms, several of them emerging within the past 24 months. The Forward Exit Option (FEO), established by Enstar, grants investors the right, in exchange for a fee, to novate residual reserves to the legacy specialist under a pricing framework fixed at inception. On exercise, investors receive liquidity and finality, and the option provider assumes the reserve development risk and faces the cedent from that point on. The FEO made its debut in Starwind Specialty’s Fractal Re sidecar, and Enstar has said it is being positioned for broader use, including in property sidecars,” AM Best said.

The agency continued: “Scheduled commutations build the exit into the contract from the start; Enstar’s Scaur Hill Re, for example, gives investors an optional commutation at year seven and a mandatory exit at year ten, each at pre-specified pricing. After the fact, a loss portfolio transfer (LPT) moves an identified book of reserves to a legacy buyer, an adverse development cover (ADC) absorbs deterioration above a chosen attachment, and secondary sales pass investor interests to incoming investors, though volumes remain modest and pricing stays private.”

Turning attention towards QBE Re’s George Street Re casualty sidecar, which was launched at the beginning of the year, AM Best highlighted how this vehicle took a different approach. Instead of attaching an exit option to the structure, the agency noted that it placed legacy specialist Compre inside the investor base from inception alongside Culpeper Capital Partners and Calidris Investment Partners.

AM Best added that Compre participates in a defined portion of the George Street Re sidecar, helping shape the contractual terms and the collateral construct that will govern at exit, and is positioned to step into the other investors’ positions over roughly five to seven years, with the ability to take on their future liabilities annually.

AM Best further added, “In 2026, Enstar and Artex announced a partnership to embed prospective and retrospective exit solutions across Artex-managed ILS vehicles, an early step toward standardized exit engineering.”

Although these mechanisms can provide investors with liquidity or contractual finality, the agency cautioned that they do not eliminate the underlying reserve risk exposure, highlighting that their effect depends on which party retains or assumes that exposure and when any transfer occurs.

In addition, AM Best’s report outlines that the float backing these casualty vehicles is commonly invested in credit, which means that just one event, or an inflation spike or credit contraction, can hurt both sides of the vehicle at once, with reserves deteriorating while the collateral behind them loses value.

“Hurricane losses do not depend on the state of the economy, and that independence is the basis of the diversification case for traditional property ILS,” AM Best said.

Adding: “That linkage between asset values and casualty risk matters directly to AM Best’s tail risk analysis because scenarios in which a sidecar’s capital falls short may also be those in which credit-sensitive collateral is under pressure and the sponsor is less able to absorb the returning risk. The assessment applies stressed correlations between reserve and asset risks and treats illiquid collateral conservatively.”

To conclude, AM Best noted that it evaluates exit provisions to determine which party holds the reserve risk exposure after an exit is exercised within these vehicles.

“Scheduled commutations imply that reserves may return to the sponsor, so the analysis considers the likely maturity and adequacy of the reserve position at the commutation date. A pre-priced novation to a well-capitalized legacy carrier can genuinely limit the sponsor’s exposure, with the credit given tempered by counterparty strength and the enforceability of the pricing framework,” the report added.

AM Best concludes: “Public disclosure of quota-share percentages, collateral guidelines, related-party investment limits, and exit pricing remains limited even as casualty sidecars grow in number and size, and descriptions of three-year underwriting periods do not always make clear that the corresponding investment exposure can continue for considerably longer. Genuine risk transfer, high-quality and liquid collateral, credible reserving, and a clearly defined exit tend to lower the tail risk charge; aggressive loss assumptions, poor-quality or illiquid collateral, and uncertain exit provisions tend to raise it.”

Speaking earlier today during Hannover Re’s Baden-Baden media briefing, Patrick Horstmann Managing Director, and Head of insurance-linked securities (ILS) at the firm, emphasised that the German reinsurer sees ILS capital as a sustainable addition to the global reinsurance market and a key area of growth for the company.

Hannover Re has been steadily growing in the ILS market in recent years.

In late 2025, the reinsurer launched its Bermuda-based ILS platform, Hannover Re Capital Partners in late 2025, and began writing business at the January 1st 2026 reinsurance renewals to further scale its alternative capital capabilities.

“ILS capital has grown over the last years and has also grown relatively more than traditional reinsurance capital. Meanwhile, it’s roughly 18% of the overall reinsurance capacity, and we see alternative capital as a sustainable addition to the traditional capital in the market,” Horstmann explained during the briefing.

“Especially in the last year we have seen this increase. But we have seen over the long term and over the long horizon the sustainability of ILS capital in the market,” he continued.

Horstmann also outlined that Hannover Re aims to bridge capital markets and cedants, noting that the reinsurer’s ILS activities include five key businesses segments: catastrophe bond transformation, collateralized fronting, life ILS, its cat bond focused manager Leine Investment, and the company’s newest ILS venture the Hannover Re Capital Partners (HCP) unit.

“Since November last year, we have launched an insurance agent in Bermuda called Hannover Re Capital Partners, and that is a platform where we connect third-party capital with the risk, utilising our Hannover Re underwriting, modeling, structuring expertise, and so enabling third-party investors to access traditional reinsurance risk with the help of Hannover Re and the support of Hannover Re,” Horstmann added.

During the Q&A portion, Horstmann provided more detail on HCP.

The executive said the platform is “not a risk-carrying entity” and uses collateralized fronting structures.

He also added that HCP has raised a low triple-digit million amount in assets under management and had fully deployed that capital for the July 1st 2026, renewal.

“At the moment, we are in discussions with further investors to raise additional capital. But I’m always a bit reluctant to give any aims or targets. What I can say is, we are fully aligned with our business plan, which we had initially.

“So we are very satisfied with the development so far and have seen a lot of interest from third-party investors in our activities, appreciating our global market access, our underwriting expertise, and also the ILS knowledge we have gained over the last decades. So we have a lot seen of interest in further discussions,” Horstmann added.

In addition, we also asked Horstmann to outline where Hannover Re sees its biggest opportunities in the capital markets and ILS sector for next year?

“Focusing on the five pillars we have within ILS at Hannover Re, I would say we have a very good market footprint for catastrophe bond transformation and for the collateralized fronting business. So we expect them in the next year, or the next two years, to be stable, potentially slightly growing,” Horstmann said.

Adding: “We have been compared to the market as a bit underrepresented in terms of third-party asset management, so Leine Investment and Hannover Re Capital Partners. So, just because our footprint in the market was not as strong there as for the other areas, I would expect there to be more growth in absolute and on relative terms compared to the other segments.”

We also asked Thorsten Steinmann, CEO, E+S Rück, member of the Executive Board, Hannover Re, whether the reinsurer has any plans in place to look at other opportunities to share risk with investor markets in the near future.

“We’ve always said in the last few weeks because one of those topics which came up is the topic of casualty sidecars, and this is partially done via Lloyd’s partially directly via investors, and this is a space where we are very cautious and we are not playing in this space.

“It’s not part of our product that we are offering to our clients, simply because we believe that the complexity of this long tail business, in combination with the asset management risk that you run, that we are very cautious to play in this field. I’m not saying this is going to be the case forever, but the response today is that we are very cautious and observing,” Steinmann explained. 

Hannover Re sees ILS capital as sustainable reinsurance addition, source of growth: Horstmann was published by: www.Artemis.bm

Franklin Templeton Investment Solutions, the hedge fund-focused arm of the global asset manager, has moderated its stance on the catastrophe bonds asset class slightly from ‘strongly overweight’ to ‘overweight’ for Q4 2026, which in turn has led the firm to shift its stance on the insurance-linked securities market to ‘neutral’.

At the same time, the firm’s neutral stance on other insurance-linked securities (ILS), including private collateralized reinsurance, retrocession, and industry loss warranties (ILWs), remains unchanged.

It’s important to remember that “overweight” on catastrophe bonds remains very positive and means the investment managers continues to see the opportunity in the cat bond asset class as meaningful for portfolios.

Commenting on the cat bond market’s performance in the third quarter of 2026, Franklin Templeton said, “Although there were several notable catastrophe events in August, none resulted in major insured losses affecting the cat bond market. Combined with seasonal factors, cat bond prices stayed strong as the market approached the peak of the Atlantic hurricane season.”

Franklin Templeton also acknowledged that global insured catastrophe losses remained relatively moderate in the first half of 2026, with industry estimates sitting below long-term averages.

The Swiss Re Institute previously estimated that global insured losses from nat cat events reached US $42 billion in the first half of 2026, which the reinsurer said at the time, marked the lowest first-half total recorded since 2020, and 16% below the 10-year average.

In addition, Franklin Templeton noted that several key catastrophe events occurred in August, including earthquakes, floods and wildfires, but stressed that none of these resulted in major insured losses affecting the global cat bond market.

“Atlantic hurricane activity also remained subdued as the season approached its historical peak, broadly consistent with strengthening El Niño conditions. Several tropical storms developed in August, but none intensified into hurricanes. The relatively benign loss environment, seasonal factors and strong investor demand supported cat bond prices and tighter spreads heading into peak hurricane season. While activity has remained subdued, we remain cautious until the season concludes,” Franklin Templeton continued.

“Structurally, we remain constructive on cat bonds, as the market continues to expand, supported by strong investor demand and issuance from both new and returning sponsors. Furthermore, current spreads and yields remain attractive relative to high-yield bonds and the asset class continues to offer low correlation with traditional financial markets.”

Franklin Templeton’s shift on cat bonds is reflected in the firm’s conviction-focused z-score, which has now seen its score decrease from 1.1 in Q3’26, to 0.9 for Q4’26.

While a score of 0.9 sits firmly within the overweight range (defined as +0.5 to +1), cat bonds currently occupy joint second position among the manager’s conviction scores for Q4 2026. Technology leads the rankings with a score of 1.4, whereas fixed income, event-driven-special situations, and discretionary  share the second-place position, each registering a score of 0.9.

As mentioned, Franklin Templeton’s neutral stance on other insurance-linked securities (ILS) remains unchanged.

However, the manager’s conviction score for other ILS has moderately decreased from 0.4 in Q3’26, to -0.1 for Q4’26.

As we’ve alluded to before, many allocators still see a compelling investment case for catastrophe bonds, even following the recent price softening. While spreads have narrowed, attachment points and core terms and conditions have not meaningfully weakened for over three years now.

Primary catastrophe bond market activity is set for a strong final quarter in 2026, driven by expectations for a strong pipeline and how the lower spread environment may encourage more sponsors to enter the market, according to Sidney Rostan, Head of ILS Strategies at SCOR Investment Partners.

SCOR Investment Partners is the asset management arm of the French reinsurance group and a specialist manager of insurance-linked securities (ILS) funds.

In a new commentary reflecting on the insurance-linked securities market’s performance in Q3 2026, Rostan highlighted that there were no meaningful insurance losses during the period, in what he described as “a very quiet US hurricane and Japan typhoon season, with no impactful landfall to be mentioned.”

“Like every year, the primary cat bond market became relatively quiet during the summer, with no transaction issued. This brings the YTD cat bond volume issued to approximately USD 18.5 billion as of the end of Q3 2026, slightly above volume issued during the same period in 2025,” Rostan said.

“In the absence of any threats in the tropical waters, the secondary cat bond market remained quiet during the summer, with only limited volumes traded. In this context, prices moved up significantly, driven by the customary seasonality effect which is at its strongest during the height of the hurricane/typhoon season.”

However, if we include the secondary market too, Artemis’ data shows that total catastrophe bond issuance for the first nine-months of the year set a new record of $18.9 billion.

Download your free copy of Artemis’ Q3 2026 Cat Bond & ILS Market Report here, where you can read more details, including a breakdown of deal flow by features such as perils, triggers, expected loss, and pricing, as well as analysis of the issuance trends seen by month and year.

Rostan further added: “In this environment, Q4 2026 is expected to see a very busy primary market according to discussions with cat bond structurers, as the lower spread environment will encourage potential cat bond sponsors to issue bonds in the context of a continuously increasing demand for protection.”

Given this, the executive underscored that total primary cat bond market activity could break last year’s full record of $25 billion.

Rostan also added that cat bond spreads are expected to come down slightly in the fourth quarter, emphasising that the high level of primary market issuances should sustain spread levels but should be well met given the level of capacity that’s currently available in the market.

Moving beyond the cat bond market, at both the June and July reinsurance renewals in the United States, rates continued their differentiated decline, with sharper reductions seen on quality cedents’ occurrence layers and more moderate decreases on aggregate and working layers, which resulted in a -15% to -20% risk-adjusted rate change YoY.

Following this year’s Rendez-Vous de Septembre in Monte Carlo, Rostan highlighted that well-capitalised markets are setting the stage for a shifting negotiation dynamic, pointing out that participants are expecting further, though more moderate softening in property catastrophe reinsurance pricing at the January renewals, and that negotiations are likely to extend beyond pricing, with terms and conditions as well as attachment levels expected to be key areas of focus during renewal discussions.

Lastly, Rostan also highlighted that the industry loss warranty (ILW) market remained quiet during Q3 2026 with no noticeable pricing changes seen during the period.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is actively promoting catastrophe bonds for sovereign disaster risk financing across the region, but Thomas Kessler noted last week that this will require cooperation across governments, research and modelling institutions, insurers and the ILS investor base.

Speaking in Bermuda at the Convergence 2026 conference last week, Thomas Kessler, Principal Disaster Risk Insurance & Finance Specialist at the Asian Development Bank (ADB) explained that replicating its first successful catastrophe bond issuances takes time and the engagement of insurance-linked securities market participants.

As we reported back in April 2026, the Asian Development Bank’s (ADB) first catastrophe bonds delivered $160 million of capital market-backed parametric earthquake and extreme precipitation disaster risk financing, evenly split between the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan.

These were the first transactions issued by the ADB’s own treasury facilities and proved the concept of issuing what it terms Disaster Relief Bonds (DRB), benefiting two of its members and securing them efficient disaster risk financing from institutional and insurance-linked securities (ILS) investors.

Importantly, Kessler explained that these catastrophe bonds come with a very clear mandate to deliver any payouts that are triggered during their coverage terms to provide social protection for specific groups.

This is not typical of catastrophe bonds, as they more frequently are used to provide reinsurance from the capital markets to insurer or reinsurer sponsors.

But in this case the Asian Development Bank designed the risk transfer to have a clear delivery of funding to groups expected to be most affected by the covered natural disaster events.

Kessler explained that the cat bonds were structured to have defined payout procedures, that aim to direct funds to vulnerable people and also provide investors with traceable impact reporting.

The parametric triggers themselves are designed to reflect affected populations, to ensure delivery of payout liquidity to support the recovery of those in the impacted regions who need it most.

As said, the payouts are designed to reach vulnerable households in the covered countries, with that delivered through existing national social protection systems, with the added benefit of reporting and auditing to support traceability for the investors that allocated to the bonds.

Kessler told the Convergence 2026 audience, “We actually set up SOPs, standard operating procedures, with many ministries in the countries. And we made sure that children, women, elderly people, people with disabilities, who are registered under the national social protection scheme, would benefit from the payouts, and we set in place reporting and auditing procedures in order to make sure that the household would get the money in case of a payout.”

This is an innovative way to both evidence the positive impact of any payout, while also ensuring it goes to those most in need of financial support when disaster strike.

It shows a way ILS structures can be designed to provide auditable impact, something that aligns well with the motivations of any sovereign sponsor and with many investors.

Kessler said, “This was highly appreciated by most of the investors, because it’s really the first time that we increased the transparency and the traceability of such an instrument, and we provided the investors with measurable SDG impact.

“Another unique feature is the triggers of these parametric bonds. So both earthquake and extreme precipitation were linked to the number of affected people, because they are eventually the beneficiary.”

Kessler also highlighted that the ADB created a web interface through which both the government’s and the investors could look at the modelling and monitor the impacts of perils, again an innovative feature of these cat bond deals.

Having completed its first catastrophe bond issuances, the ADB is now keen to replicate these deals and encourage other regional governments to look to disaster risk transfer as a valuable source of protection.

“ADB will further promote disaster relief bonds in Asia and the Pacific. We want to replicate them, take the momentum, and we’d like to have a regional approach,” Kessler explained.

“So we look at areas such as the Pacific Islands, which are faced with above average expected loss. We’re looking at Southeast Asia, the ASEAN, which combines large economies, further developed and also very small. We’re looking at the Hindu Kush Himalaya, you have seen the events in Nepal, Bhutan. And of course, we’re going to continue to work in in the CAREC region.

“So with this, we will provide opportunities for investors to diversify their portfolios geographically as well as into new risks, and we also hope that investors will get acquainted to new regions.”

Kessler closed by saying, “We can’t do it without cooperation between government, between academia, research institutions, science, modellers, structurers and the investors. MDBs, like the Asian Development Bank, can bring them all together.

“This leaves me with the saying: If you want to go fast you can go alone, but if you’re going to go far let’s go together, and let’s make an impact which is urgent.”
